<description>
**Problem:** Block and undo writers buffer serialized data, then rely on the `BufferedWriter` destructor to write the remaining bytes.
`fwrite()` can report fewer bytes written than requested after a local storage error, e.g., if the filesystem fills up while a block is being written (my 1 TB benchmarking servers have recently been filling up, so I've been seeing these failures more often).
`AutoFile::write_buffer()` converts that result into an exception, and because the destructor is implicitly non-throwing, the exception invokes `std::terminate`.
Calling `flush()` before destruction is insufficient on its own because a failed flush leaves the same bytes pending, so the destructor retries the write while the original exception unwinds.

I introduced this bug in #31551 when adding `BufferedWriter`.

I’d update the **Fix** section to include `discard()` and describe exactly what the destructor checks. The problem statement and reproducer can stay as written.

**Fix:** Block and undo writers now flush explicitly before destruction.
If serialization or writing throws `std::ios_base::failure`, they discard any pending bytes, log the error, close the file, and request shutdown through the existing fatal-error path.
`BufferedWriter` clears the pending byte count before writing because the stream may obfuscate the bytes in place and a short write may already have put some of them on disk, making a retry unsafe.
The destructor uses `Assume` to check that no bytes are pending before attempting a fallback flush.
`flush()` continues to propagate exceptions, and `AutoFile` remains unchanged.

Manual write-error reproducer

Force the error path in `AutoFile::write_buffer()`:

```sh
sed -i '' '/^.*AutoFile::write_buffer(/,/^}/s/!= src.size()/!= 0/' src/streams.cpp
cmake -B build && cmake --build build -j5 && build/bin/bitcoind -regtest -datadir="$(mktemp -d)"; echo "exit=$?"
```

Before this change, implicit flushing invokes `std::terminate`:

[quoted text omitted]
With this change, `bitcoind` logs the write failure, then completes normal shutdown and exits with status 1:

[quoted text omitted]
</description>

That's true in debug builds, where the destructor's `Assume` aborts. Release builds normally don't crash: the destructor writes the partial record and the exception continues to the caller, as on master. Either seems fine for a case that shouldn't happen.

What `discard()` changes is the I/O error path: the `catch` drops whatever is pending itself, so it no longer depends on `flush()` having cleared the buffer before it threw, and the destructor's `Assume` checks a contract the class states (finish with `flush()` or `discard()`) rather than something only a failed `flush()` can do.

[quoted text omitted]
I'm not sure I follow this one. If the `flush()` inside the `try` fails, the `catch` calls `discard()`, and the destructor's `flush()` has nothing left to write. If you mean a path that leaves the scope without calling `flush()` or `discard()` (the interrupt case I mentioned), then yes: the destructor's fallback flush can still fail and terminate, and the `Assume` is there to catch such paths in debug builds.

[quoted text omitted]
I think the main goal here is the `BufferedWriter` interface, and I'm fine with any error handling at the two call sites that isn't worse than master. Making the two call sites handle errors the same way (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36049#discussion_r4684762185) and a general pattern for this class of problem (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36049#discussion_r4605579266) both seem fine as follow-ups.

```cpp
BOOST_AUTO_TEST_CASE(buffered_writer_discard)
{
    struct CountingStream {
        int write_attempts{0};
        void write_buffer(std::span<std::byte>) { ++write_attempts; }
    } stream;
    {
        BufferedWriter writer{stream, 4};
        writer.write("00"_hex);
        writer.discard();
    }
    BOOST_CHECK_EQUAL(stream.write_attempts, 0);

```
[2026-11-24] rc:4684326033 inline on src/streams.h by ryanofsky (member) (edited 2026-11-24):
re: l0rinc https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36049#discussion_r4606518586

[quoted text omitted]
A follow-up sounds right for deciding and implementing it. For reference, I think the options are roughly these:

1. Keep explicit `flush()` and `discard()` calls, as in this PR and like `AutoFile::fclose()`, and add a `bitcoin-tidy` check that every path out of a writer's scope calls one of them. Today a missed call is at least caught at runtime by the destructor's `Assume` in debug builds.
2. Have the destructor discard pending bytes automatically while an exception is unwinding (comparing `std::uncaught_exceptions()` with its value at construction), and keep requiring an explicit `flush()` on the normal path, checked by the `Assume` as now. Error paths would no longer need a `discard()` call. A `bitcoin-tidy` check would also be simpler than for option 1, since it would only need to check normal exits, not which calls can throw.
3. Let the destructor flush on the normal path and throw if that fails (`noexcept(false)`, the Cap'n Proto approach from my comment above), and discard when another exception is already unwinding. Callers wouldn't need any explicit calls, but a writer held in a container or destroyed in a `noexcept` function would turn errors back into `std::terminate`, so this would need a `bitcoin-tidy` check too.
4. Replace the explicit calls with a helper that takes a callback, like `WriteBuffered(file, [&](auto& writer) { writer << ...; })`, which flushes after the callback returns and discards if it throws. Callers can't forget either call, but the writes have to fit in a lambda.

re: maflcko https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36049#discussion_r4610421734

[quoted text omitted]
Yes agree this could still be a good idea
[2026-11-24] rc:4684762185 inline on src/node/blockstorage.cpp by ryanofsky (member) (edited 2026-11-24):
In commit "blockstorage: discard buffered bytes on I/O errors" (1584299ae51d5c0bb821f4f51521ec6eaf9bdfbd)

Not important, and fine to leave as is, but since `WriteBlock`'s callers already catch `std::runtime_error` around it ([`AcceptBlock`](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/1584299ae51d5c0bb821f4f51521ec6eaf9bdfbd/src/validation.cpp#L4461-L4463) calls `FatalError`, and [`LoadGenesisBlock`](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/1584299ae51d5c0bb821f4f51521ec6eaf9bdfbd/src/validation.cpp#L5040-L5043) fails init), I think the simplest and most straightforward way of dealing with errors here would be for this `catch` to only clean up and rethrow:

```cpp
} catch (...) {
    fileout.discard();
    (void)file.fclose();
    throw;
}
```

This way errors thrown while writing are all handled by callers instead of a subset of them handled here and others handled by callers. This would be closer to how write errors were handled before #31551, when they were thrown straight out of `WriteBlock`, and `AcceptBlock` would report the write error itself instead of adding a misleading "Failed to find position to write new block to disk".

`WriteBlockUndo` is different: nothing between it and the [`catch` blocks in `ProcessMessages`](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/1584299ae51d5c0bb821f4f51521ec6eaf9bdfbd/src/net_processing.cpp#L5491-L5495) handles exceptions, so a rethrown undo write error would only be logged at debug level and the node would keep running, as it did before #31551. So I think `WriteBlockUndo` should keep its own `FatalError` handler for now.

Ideally a follow-up would make `WriteBlock` and `WriteBlockUndo` consistent: either add a `std::runtime_error` catch around the `WriteBlockUndo` call too, so both functions can clean up and rethrow, or handle every error inside `WriteBlock` and drop the catches in its callers.

Code review ACK 1584299ae51d5c0bb821f4f51521ec6eaf9bdfbd. It also replaces the `std::terminate` on a failed block or undo write (for example a full disk) with a logged error and a shutdown.

Thanks for taking the two commits, and sorry that part of my earlier suggestion was based on bad assumptions: I proposed narrowing these `catch` blocks to `std::ios_base::failure` without understanding how the callers handle exceptions or the context around this code. Nothing in these blocks throws anything else today, so I don't think it causes a problem, and I still think `discard()` itself is right.

On the error handling in `WriteBlock` and `WriteBlockUndo`, I'm fine with any of the approaches discussed here as long as the behavior isn't worse than master, where any write error terminates. The error handling around these calls was inconsistent before this PR and still is, and I think that's a separate problem from the `BufferedWriter` interface, which is the main improvement here.
